correctness.rationale: The only centered balls have sizes 1, 4 and 6. On nonnegative inputs the squared maximal quotient is the maximum of the squared row-selection quotients; nonnegative Gram matrices allow a nonnegative top eigenvector, so no row-activity restriction is needed for the upper bound. Independently enumerated all 729 assignments by graph distances in /workspace/checks/replay_k33.py. For A the selected averaging matrix, the independent integer Bareiss check of 5616 I − 25(12A)^T(12A) established positive leading minors for exactly 727 assignments. The exceptions are (0,0,0,1,1,1) and its exchange. The 55 canonical selections and the six listed minima on the 54 strict types were reproduced exactly. On the exceptional assignment the mean-zero directions have squared singular values 1 and 1/16, each twice, and the class-constant Gram block is [[1,3],[3,25]]/16. Its top eigenvalue is simple, exceeds 39/25, and has positive vector (sqrt(17)−4,1); direct comparison confirms radius one is strictly active on the smaller class and radius zero on the larger. Thus the value and both labeled rays, as well as coordinate sign freedom, follow. The decimal 1.25919907274557… is correct. For general r the class-constant two-by-two block proves the attained test quotient B_r; the positive optimizer has 0<a<b since the largest eigenvalue exceeds 1 (test a=0) and a≥b gives quotient ≤1. Increasing r strictly improves its lower-class average, and the limiting matrix has norm sqrt(2). This does not prove full-norm sharpness for r≥4. Inspected the uploaded verification and script; the reproduction used independent code, not that script.

value.rationale: The first cubic balanced biclique is a natural highly symmetric strong-norm test beyond the four-cycle and unlike stars or complete graphs. Rigidity shows exactly when the class-constant lower test captures the nonlinear operator despite the global ball, supplying a useful exact comparison with the cubic cube. The balanced family gives a monotone lower comparison approaching sqrt(2), without claiming an unsupported upper bound. The finite certificate decides a well-motivated exact invariant, not an arbitrary enumeration.
